paper_title: Consensus Capture in Reference-Based UAV Video Stabilization: A Benchmark on Dynamic Urban Scenes

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reference-frame stabilization registers every frame of a hovering-drone video onto one reference frame, keeping object positions comparable. The registration pipelines it relies on are selected on feature-matching benchmarks in which only the camera moves. Over a busy intersection, vehicles moving together supply mutually consistent correspondences that can draw the robust homography estimate toward their motion: consensus capture, which inlier statistics cannot flag. A two-part benchmark measures it and the object masking meant to prevent it. A static protocol scores ten pipelines under exactly known homographies on 4K aerial frames, tuned on a site-disjoint split at a matched resolution and feature budget. A dynamic protocol scores them at an offline and a real-time budget on hovers selected from the video alone to span the amount and coherence of moving foreground, plus a stationary control. It measures background alignment, object position error and the share of a moving group's displacement an estimate follows, against a pseudo-ground-truth reference audited with manually annotated ground control points, which also score every candidate. On static scenes, tuned AKAZE, RootSIFT, SIFT and BRISK lead, retuning the matcher thresholds raises the mean average accuracy (mAA) by at most 0.0062, and masking costs less than 0.005. Unmasked ORB is captured on 28 of 304 real-time dynamic pairs and on 6 offline; its real-time captured estimates have a median corner error of 18.8 px yet typical inlier counts and ratios. Masking removes capture for every pipeline and leaves the leading pipelines unchanged. Code, data and results are released.

Keywords: UAV video stabilization, image registration, homography estimation, feature matching, oriented bounding box, traffic monitoring 1. Introduction Reference-frame stabilization is the registration model used when object positions must stay consistent over long hover, during which wind keeps shifting and rotating the view: every frame is aligned directly onto one fixed reference frame, so that error does not accumulate and position measured in frame is comparable with one measured minutes earlier. Trajectory extraction from high-altitude unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) video is the application studied here, and traffic monitoring supplies the footage, but the requirement is shared by any analysis that compares moving objects across time in image or map coordinates, such as river surface velocimetry (Ljubiˇcic et al., 2021). The estimate is homography, and the pipeline that produces it (feature detector, descriptor, matcher, robust estimator, and, where objects are annotated, masking strategy that withholds them from feature detection) is assembled from components each of which has been benchmarked extensively (Efe et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2021; Barath et al., 2023). Those benchmarks evaluate correspondence accuracy on scenes without independently moving content: planar surfaces, landmark facades, building walls. The only source of disagreement between their two views is the camera. hovering drone over busy intersection presents the opposite case. The camera barely moves, and dozens of objects in the frame move without it, many of them together: platoon released by green light translates as unit, and every vehicle in it supplies correspondences that agree with one another under single transform, the one describing their motion. If those correspondences win the consensus, the robust estimator does not fail. It solves the problem it was posed, returning homography that is internally consistent and well supported but describes the vehicles rather than the road  (Fig. 1)  . We call this failure consensus capture, and it has consequence for evaluation before it has one for method design. Inlier count, inlier ratio, and reprojection error measure the self-consistency of fit, and coherently moving foreground Corresponding author. Both panels show the same zoomed-in crop of the 3840 2160 frame, centered on the largest moving group; orange boxes are the vehicles that moved together between the two frames, with their motion. The estimate registers the group back onto where it stood (capture fraction 0.96), so its error, drawn as black arrows on grid and magnified by the factor in the legend, carries the platoons motion across the whole crop (10.0 px corner error against the reference estimator), while 23 % of its 466 inliers lie on the moving vehicles (orange dots). Both are re-registered with the stored parameters and seed of the real-time campaign (Section 7.3). is self-consistent by construction. Where it wins, these quantities are no longer merely weak proxies for accuracy, as they are already known to be on static scenes (Jin et al., 2021; Barath et al., 2023); they become anti-informative, because the moving-object consensus can be the cleaner of the two available fits. An evaluation that reads them cannot detect capture. What is needed scores the alignment of the static world directly, makes moving-object consensus observable, and relates it to how much of the frame moves and how coherently. To our knowledge no matching or registration benchmark provides this: none combines independently moving content with reference geometry (Section 2), so risk flagged for airborne video (Kirchhof and Stilla, 2006) has gone unmeasured. Capture matters most where trajectories are used one at time. Macroscopic quantities such as flow and density average transient offset away, but microscopic analyses read individual trajectories and their derivatives: car following, lane changes (Kim et al., 2026), per-vehicle noise emission (Espadaler-Clapés et al., 2023), and surrogate safety measures such as time-to-collision, post-encroachment time and the deceleration rate to avoid crash (Abdel-Aty et al., 2023; Espadaler-Clapés et al., 2025), which drone trajectory datasets now provide or are built to support (Zheng et al., 2024; Fonod et al., 2025a). Under reference-frame registration each frame is registered on its own, so nothing ties captured estimate to those of neighboring frames: its error follows the groups motion and is present only while the group holds the consensus. Speeds and accelerations are differences of positions over fractions of second, so an error that varies from frame to frame in this way is amplified in them (Punzo et al., 2011). The accuracy these datasets aim for is correspondingly tight: the inD dataset requires positioning error below 0.1 (Bock et al., 2020), under two pixels at the ground sample distance (GSD) of the footage studied here (Section 3), whereas the captured estimates of Section 7.3 have median corner error of 18.8 px, about meter on the ground, against the reference estimator. Since the estimates pulled toward the group keep typical inlier statistics, pipeline captured on few frames passes their error, unflagged, to every trajectory in those frames. Several of these datasets are also recorded lower than the 140 to 150 studied here: inD from up to 100 at about 4 cm per pixel (Bock et al., 2020) and the intersections of CitySim from 120 (Zheng et al., 2024); view that covers less ground can give vehicle group of the same size larger share of the frame and of its features. We provide such an evaluation in two parts. Part is static protocol under exactly known homographies and photometric degradation, on 4K frames from multi-drone experiment over Songdo, South Korea: one from each of the 29 viewpoints from which its ten drones recorded 20 intersections. It establishes what each pipeline can do when nothing moves and which of its settings matter, extending the campaign of Fonod et al. (2025a) with paired trials, per-pipeline tuning on site-disjoint split, and matched resolution and feature budget. Part II is dynamic protocol on nine hovers over busy intersections, each registered onto reference frame selected from the video alone to span the amount and coherence of moving foreground, plus stationary control that separates the removal of moving objects from the removal 2 of texture. It runs every pipeline at an offline and real-time point of Part Is budget grid. Real footage has no true homography, so Part II measures background alignment outside the annotated objects, the position error trajectory inherits, the direction of the error relative to the dominant motion, and the share of moving groups displacement an estimate follows, which measures capture where it happens. Its pseudo-ground-truth reference estimator is audited against manually annotated ground control points (GCPs) (image positions of static ground points, not surveyed coordinates), which also score every candidate directly, so that the masking comparison does not depend on the reference estimators own masking. Masking with horizontal bounding boxes (HBBs) and oriented bounding boxes (OBBs) is controlled axis throughout, since the shape of mask could matter in either direction (Section 5). On hovers over Songdo intersections, the measurement finds capture. At the real-time budget, unmasked ORB is captured in all five cases that present coherently moving group, the four with much moving foreground and the stationary control, on 28 of the 304 pairs that carry one, though 22 of them in single case. The 17 within the first second are pulls toward the group; 10 of the 11 beyond it are breakdowns of the estimate, which unmasked ORB also shows with no group in view. At the offline budget capture is rarer (unmasked ORB, 6 pairs in two cases). Estimates pulled toward group cannot be told apart by their inlier statistics: their inlier counts and ratios match those of the same pipeline at the nearest offsets of the same case, at both budgets. Masking removes capture for every pipeline at both budgets while leaving the leading pipelines, SIFT, RootSIFT and AKAZE, where they were; for real-time ORB, whose feature budget it also returns to the ground, the captured pairs can account for at most quarter of the gain. HBBs and OBBs do not differ at these densities and orientations, where the two geometries withhold nearly the same pixels. Averaged over all nine cases, four of which never present moving group, the masking benefit is either not significant or smaller than the repeatability of the GCPs (Section 7.5). The conclusions are bounded by the moving share of these cases; the protocol is not, and it applies unchanged to footage from lower altitude or over denser traffic, where that share is larger. 1.1. Contributions 1. benchmark for the complete registration pipeline of reference-based UAV stabilization in dynamic urban scenes: static protocol under exactly known homographies (Section 6) and dynamic protocol on real hovering-drone footage at an offline and real-time compute budget (Section 7). It covers the pipelines deployed stabilization library exposes, as measurement of that system rather than leaderboard of state-of-the-art matchers (Section 3.2). 2. An evaluation methodology for dynamic scenes, where self-consistency statistics are unreliable: backgroundalignment measures that need no ground-truth homography, object-level errors that bound the position error trajectory inherits, two measures that make consensus capture observable (the direction of the error and the share of moving groups displacement an estimate follows), and GCP audit that measures the error of the pseudo-ground truth and supplies an independent comparison (Section 4), under pre-specified analysis plan (Section 4.9). 3. case-selection procedure that measures from the video alone how much of the foreground moves, how coherently, and when, and chooses the cases and their reference frames to span these conditions, under which capture can arise; its measurements are validated against published vehicle trajectories (Section 7.1). 4. measurement of consensus capture and of object-aware masking on real footage: at the real-time budget unmasked ORB is captured in every case that presents coherent group, its pull toward the group is invisible to inlier statistics, and capture disappears under masking at detection (Sections 7.3 and 7.5). 5. The public release of the benchmark implementation (Fonod, 2026c) and of its data (Fonod and Geroliminis, 2026a) (annotated frames, cases, GCPs and every campaigns results), from which every benchmark number is regenerated by command. Also released are hbb2obb (Fonod, 2026b), the SAM-assisted conversion of HBBs to OBBs that makes OBB masks available at benchmark scale, and Songdo Vision OBB (Fonod and Geroliminis, 2026b), the OBB version of Songdo Vision (Fonod et al., 2026), together with the human-verified oriented reference against which the conversion is validated (Section 5.1 and Appendix E). 2. Related work Local features and matching. Correspondence estimation has been surveyed repeatedly as it moved from hand-crafted operators to learned ones (Ma et al., 2021). The pipelines benchmarked here span three generations of that work. Hand-crafted detectors and descriptors, from SIFT (Lowe, 2004) and its RootSIFT normalization (Arandjelovic and Zisserman, 2012) to the binary ORB (Rublee et al., 2011) and BRISK (Leutenegger et al., 2011) and the nonlinear scale spaces of KAZE (Alcantarilla et al., 2012) and AKAZE (Alcantarilla et al., 2013), remain the default in deployed stabilization pipelines, because they need no training data, no accelerator, and no assumption about the imagery. Learned detectors and descriptors replace one or both stages with network trained for repeatability and matchability, among them 3 SuperPoint (DeTone et al., 2018), DISK (Tyszkiewicz et al., 2020), DeDoDe (Edstedt et al., 2024a), Key.Net (BarrosoLaguna et al., 2019) and XFeat (Potje et al., 2024); learned matchers such as LightGlue (Lindenberger et al., 2023) replace the nearest-neighbor search and its ratio test with attention over the two keypoint sets; and detector-free methods such as LoFTR (J. Sun et al., 2021) drop keypoints and match dense features directly. Dense matchers such as RoMa (Edstedt et al., 2024b) go further and estimate warp and its certainty for every pixel, from which correspondences are sampled. stabilization pipeline is chosen as whole and its components interact (a matcher accepts only certain descriptors, detector-free method has no keypoint budget), so the comparison of Section 6.2 spans all three. Two properties of this literature shape the protocol. Orientation estimation is not universal, so several learned models are effectively upright, which is why rotation is swept, as Tareen and Saleem (2018) sweep it for the classical detectors, which they find unequally invariant to it; and the input resolution of learned model is memory bound rather than free choice, which is why the compute budget is an axis of the benchmark. Direct homography regression. parallel line of work regresses the transform from an image pair (DeTone et al., 2016). Zhang et al. (2020) observe that loss computed uniformly over the image cannot keep moving or non-planar objects from contributing to it, and learn content mask that rejects those regions: the problem measured here, approached by learning what to ignore instead of by annotating it. These methods lie outside the feature-based family deployed in the trajectory extraction systems of Section 2. Robust estimation and dominant structure. RANSAC (Fischler and Bolles, 1981) and its modern variants (Barath and Matas, 2018; Barath et al., 2020) make homography recoverable from contaminated correspondences. That coherent structure of outliers can capture the consensus is known (Stewart, 1997), and Chum et al. (2005) detect dominant plane inside the estimator; Section 4.1 explains why that defense does not transfer to coherently moving group. Filters that prune matches before the estimator rest on similar vote: S. Jiang and W. Jiang (2018) keep matches whose motion agrees in direction and length, Zhou et al. (2024) build local motion consensus into learned matcher, and the motions of coherently moving group agree as well. Scenes with more than one structure. Multi-model fitting accepts that scene may contain several coherent structures and recovers them jointly, by clustering correspondences (Toldo and Fusiello, 2008; Wong et al., 2011) or by fitting instances progressively inside the robust estimator (Barath and Matas, 2019). Vehicles crossing an intersection are such second structure, and AdelaideRMF (Wong et al., 2011) does contain independently moving content. These methods are evaluated by how well correspondences are partitioned among structures, not by the accuracy of one recovered transform, and AdelaideRMF supplies no reference homography for the background. Recovering several homographies also leaves open which one describes the ground, which correspondence counts cannot decide when the moving structure is the larger. Multi-model fitting is remedy that changes the estimator; what is missing first is measurement of the failure under the estimators actually deployed. Benchmarks for matching and homography estimation. Comparative studies of classical detectors and descriptors (Tareen and Saleem, 2018) and HPatches (Balntas et al., 2017) established the vocabulary this field still uses, and Schonberger et al. (2017) set the pattern of judging hand-crafted and learned features on common downstream task. Three benchmarks set the methodological standard we adopt. Jin et al. (2021) argue that local features must be judged by downstream task rather than by intermediate proxies, and show that carefully tuned classical pipelines remain competitive with learned ones, conclusion Efe et al. (2021) reach on HPatches by optimizing single parameter; Barath et al. (2023) contribute large-scale homography benchmark with an explicit tuning-and-test protocol. Their shared lesson is that comparison is only as meaningful as the care taken to place every method on equal footing (Section 4.7). None of them measures registration accuracy on scene whose content moves independently of the camera  (Table 1)  , because their reference geometry, structure from motion (SfM) or manually labeled correspondences on static structure, must exclude independently moving objects to work at all. Registration benchmarks that do model change place it between acquisitions (T. Sun et al., 2025). Pseudo-ground truth has further cost: Brachmann et al. (2021) show that the algorithm generating it can reorder the methods evaluated against it, which is why the reference estimator of Part II is audited against GCPs (Section 4.8). Suppressing moving objects before geometry is estimated. Excluding independently moving content before geometric model is fitted is established practice in dynamic simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM). DynaSLAM (Bescos et al., 2018) and DS-SLAM (C. Yu et al., 2018) segment likely-moving classes and withhold those regions from tracking and mapping. Both report that suppression keeps the estimate usable in populated scenes; what is missing is measurement. Isolating the effect needs the masking strategy varied as controlled axis while everything else is held fixed (Section 7.5), and metric that does not read the objects themselves (Section 4.3). Video stabilization as different objective. Stabilization also names work whose goal is pleasant camera path rather than fixed frame of reference: smoothing the path under geometric constraints (Grundmann et al., 2011), over mesh of local homographies (Liu et al., 2013), or by learning the warp (J. Yu and Ramamoorthi, 2020). Its measures (cropping ratio, distortion, frequency-domain stability score) follow from perceptual objective, and none asks where pixel actually is. smoothed path may drift from any particular frame, which is inadmissible when object positions are compared across recording, and mesh of local warps can absorb independent object motion instead of rejecting it. Moving objects enter this literature as threat to the global motion estimate, met by adaptive RANSAC (Choi et al., 2009), clustered motion vectors (R. Wu et al., 2021) or foreground trajectories (Zhao and Ling, 2019), and scored by the similarity of the output frames, not against reference geometry. Registration and stabilization of aerial video. Registering airborne video to fixed reference is long established in photogrammetry (Kumar et al., 2001). The remote sensing literature on image registration concentrates on matching across modalities, sensors and acquisition times (Geng et al., 2025), with structural or phase-congruency descriptors built to be insensitive to radiometric change (Ye et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020) and networks trained on large multimodal datasets (P. Wu et al., 2026), so transient content is nuisance to be removed rather than property to be measured. Moving traffic in airborne registration. Vehicle measurement from the air rests on this registration (Karimi Nejadasl et al., 2006; Reinartz et al., 2006), and moving traffic is recognized hazard to it. Kirchhof and Stilla (2006) warn that many objects moving in the same direction, as on dense roads, can survive RANSAC and bias the homography, and exclude points at detected motion. Karimi Nejadasl and Lindenbergh (2014) rule out direct SIFT with RANSAC against the first image of helicopter sequence, in part because of the moving vehicles, and chain consecutive homographies instead. Ljubiˇcic et al. (2021) compare seven stabilization tools on UAV river footage, where the water moves and the banks do not, by residual motion at static features. None of these measures capture or what it costs in position. Aerial detection benchmarks and trajectory datasets. Aerial object detection has well-established benchmarks (Ding et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2022), DOTA made OBBs standard for aerial objects, and UAVid (Lyu et al., 2020) separates moving from static cars in 4K UAV video for semantic segmentation. They evaluate recognition, not the registration that must precede any use of object positions when the camera moves. Drone-based trajectory datasets show the dependency most clearly: pNEUMA (Barmpounakis and Geroliminis, 2020), inD (Bock et al., 2020), CitySim (Zheng et al., 2024) and Songdo Traffic (Fonod et al., 2025a) all extract positions from hovering footage after registration step, whose error georeferenced positions (Novikov et al., 2024) inherit directly, and the intersections they are recorded over are where moving-object consensus is most likely. UAV stabilization for traffic monitoring. The work closest to this paper is Fonod et al. (2025a), which extracts georeferenced vehicle trajectories from hovering-drone recordings of urban intersections and stabilizes each frame onto reference frame with an object-masked homography, releasing that stage as stabilo (Fonod, 2026d) and its parameter study as stabilo-optimize. The vehicles are masked to keep correspondences on moving objects out of the fit, the failure this paper names consensus capture, but the pipeline was selected on static scenes under synthetic warps, so neither that failure nor what masking does about it was measured on the recordings. That is the gap addressed here: the static campaign is extended (Section 6) and paired with dynamic one on the footage the pipeline is deployed on (Section 7), where the masking axis can be measured rather than assumed. 3. Problem setting Scene and platform assumptions. Recordings come from hovering drones at approximately constant altitude (140 to 150 m) in birds-eye view (BEV) at 4K resolution (3840 2160), so inter-frame motion is small and wind-induced. The ground sample distance (GSD) is about 5.5 cm per pixel: the scale of the homographies that register hovers of this experiment onto its georeferenced orthophoto (Fonod et al., 2025a) ranges from 0.0548 to 0.0564 per pixel over eleven hovers. pixel of registration error is thus about 5.5 cm on the ground, and the 5 px upper limit of the accuracy interval below is about 28 cm. Every pixel quantity in this paper converts at that rate. The stabilization model is reference-frame homography, which holds the static scene in place over hover exactly only where that scene is planar. Above-ground structures (buildings, poles, vegetation) depart from the plane in proportion to how far the platform translates; hovering platform translates little but does drift, so the evaluation excludes buildings and large tree canopy, the largest such structures, by polygons drawn on each reference frame (Section 4.3) and scores the rest of the static scene. The deployed regime is hovering platform, so the geometric perturbation pipeline has to recover in practice is few pixels of drift and fraction of degree of yaw per frame relative to the reference, growing slowly over recording. Part samples wider regime than that, so that pipelines operating limits are measured, and Section 6 states where the two regimes differ. 3.1. Component-wise evaluation is the norm in the matching literature, but the quantity stabilization system delivers is the transform, and the interactions between the axes, particularly between µ and rob, are what this benchmark is designed to expose. The components come from two libraries: the classical detectors and descriptors and every robust estimator are OpenCVs, and the learned detectors, descriptors and matchers are kornias (Riba et al., 2020). Both are driven through stabilo (Fonod, 2026d), the stabilization library of Fonod et al. (2025a), which this benchmark evaluates and does not modify. Which implementation supplies component is part of what is compared, for the reason given below. Selection of pipelines. The detector axis holds ten pipelines. Five are classical, matched by brute force with ratio test: ORB (Rublee et al., 2011), SIFT (Lowe, 2004), RootSIFT (Arandjelovic and Zisserman, 2012), BRISK (Leutenegger et al., 2011) and AKAZE (Alcantarilla et al., 2013). Four are learned and sparse: DISK (Tyszkiewicz et al., 2020), DeDoDe (Edstedt et al., 2024a) and Key.Net (Barroso-Laguna et al., 2019) (KeyNet in the tables), each matched by LightGlue (Lindenberger et al., 2023), and XFeat (Potje et al., 2024), matched by brute force because the librarys LightGlue has no weights for it. One is detector-free, LoFTR (J. Sun et al., 2021), which has no keypoint budget to set. The deployed library exposes one more detector, KAZE (Alcantarilla et al., 2012), which is left out: AKAZE is its accelerated variant, and it is the slowest classical detector by wide margin. Otherwise, the set is everything the library exposes, which is the inclusion criterion: the object of study is the system trajectory-extraction pipeline actually runs and the alternatives practitioner can select between by configuration alone, not the state of the art in matching at large. Methods outside that system, such as SuperPoint (DeTone et al., 2018) and the dense matchers of Section 2, fall outside this scope; nothing in the protocol depends on the method, and it applies to them unchanged. Robust estimators are identified by implementation, not by name. The rob axis sweeps nine OpenCV method codes spanning seven algorithms: LMEDS (Rousseeuw, 1984), RANSAC (Fischler and Bolles, 1981), RHO (Bazargani et al., 2018), GC-RANSAC (Barath and Matas, 2018), PROSAC (Chum and Matas, 2005), MAGSAC++ (Barath et al., 2020), and LO-RANSAC (Chum et al., 2003) in three configurations that differ in local-optimization iterations and in whether they run in parallel, the last four within OpenCVs implementation of the USAC framework (Raguram et al., 2013). They are reported under OpenCVs flag names with the algorithm in parentheses, because the three LO-RANSAC configurations are separate entries practitioner selects from, and because two of the flags are widely described as DEGENSAC, including in the documentation of the library evaluated here, although neither carries the dominant-plane check of Chum et al. (2005) into homography estimate (Section 4.1). Following Barath et al. (2023), method is fixed by its implementation and version rather than by its published name (Appendix A). Masking acts on feature detection. The order is: detection or segmentation mask construction feature detection description matching robust estimation. No keypoint inside mask reaches matching, so metrics defined on removed features or on dynamic inlier ratio are not applicable here, and are not used. Where the mask enters the detector differs between implementations, and it decides what masking can do under feature budget; every detector is used with the masking its implementation provides, unmodified. ORB, BRISK and AKAZE detect outside the mask and then keep their strongest responses up to the budget, so the keypoints mask removes are replaced by others. SIFT, as OpenCV implements it, keeps its strongest responses over the whole frame and then drops those inside the mask; the learned detectors accept no mask, so the library drops their selected keypoints that fall inside it. For both, masking can only remove keypoints. 4. Evaluation methodology This section shows why the internal statistics of robust fit cannot rank pipelines on dynamic scene and defines what replaces them: the metrics, the treatment of failures, comparability, the audit of the reference estimator, and the analysis plan. 4.1. Why internal-consistency metrics are insufficient Inlier count, inlier ratio, and reprojection error measure the internal consistency of fit: how well the correspondences the estimator retained agree with the model fitted to them. On static scenes they are already known to be weak proxies for accuracy. Barath et al. (2023) report that the inlier count depends on image resolution, on the inlier threshold and on the estimator, so that MAGSAC returns far more inliers than its competitors at comparable pose accuracy, and in the tabulation of Jin et al. Placing pipelines on equal footing benchmark that compares ten pipelines at one shared set of matcher settings measures the settings as much as the pipelines. This is the central methodological finding of the benchmarks reviewed in Section 2, and we adopt their remedies. Two hyperparameters are tuned per pipeline. The ratio-test threshold and the inlier threshold of the robust estimator are both known to be decisive and to have method-specific optima: the first thresholds descriptor distance distribution, property of the descriptor, and the second reprojection residual, property of keypoint localization accuracy. Efe et al. (2021) obtain their entire result by varying the first; Jin et al. (2021, Sec. 5.3) find its optimum differs per feature. They are swept jointly rather than sequentially (the inlier threshold alone where the matcher applies no ratio test: LightGlue and LoFTR), following Barath et al. (2023): looser ratio test admits more outliers, which moves the inlier threshold that best separates them, so the sequential optimum need not be the joint one. Selection uses Eq. (9), the quantity the benchmark ranks on, because the threshold maximizing correspondence-level accuracy is not the one maximizing homography accuracy: robust estimator turns surplus of looser matches into better fit (Efe et al., 2021). It is also conservative: pipeline keeps the values its preset carries unless the best grid point beats them on mAA by more than the equivalence margin of 0.01 (Section 4.9), because where the optimum is flat the best grid point only moves the values within set the data cannot tell apart; Part II starts from Part Is values in the same way. The remaining estimator parameters are fixed, on published grounds. Of the three parameters every robust estimator here exposes, the confidence level, the inlier threshold and an iteration cap, only the threshold is tuned. Jin et al. (2021, Sec. 5.1) find the confidence value to be the least sensitive of the three and fix it at 1 106, the value used here. The iteration cap is time budget rather than an accuracy parameter, and the benchmarks we follow treat it as one: Barath et al. (2023) fix it at 1000 while grid-searching the thresholds and sweep it only to draw timeaccuracy curve, and Jin et al. (2021) set it from per-pair time budget. We fix it at 5000, where it is not the binding constraint, and report wall-clock time so that no pipeline gains accuracy through unreported computation. All remaining parameters are held at documented values across pipelines (Appendix A). Tuning and evaluation scenes are disjoint. The sweep runs on scenes held out from every reported result, split the benchmarks tooling enforces: threshold chosen on the data number is reported on measures how much tuning freedom each pipeline was granted, and Barath et al. (2023) name the lack of such split as drawback of earlier homography datasets. The split is by site, not by frame: the Part set holds eight intersections recorded by more than one drone, near-duplicate views of the same road layout, markings and parked vehicles, so frame-wise split would leak the evaluation scenes into the tuning half. Every third site in alphabetical order goes to tuning, which reproduces the split from the file names alone. Of the 29 scenes, 9 from 7 sites tune and 20 from 13 sites evaluate. Part II keeps the split: its evaluation cases are drawn from evaluation sites and its own tuning cases from tuning sites. Tuning is run with masking disabled and the same parameters are used under every masking mode, so no mode is tuned into its own best configuration; because the deployed configuration is masked, this is the conservative choice for the masking comparison, and any advantage measured for masking is measured with parameters tuned against it. The compute budget is fixed before anything is tuned. Two further parameters, the downsampling ratio and the feature budget, decide how much work pipeline does rather than how it uses it, and the shipped presets do not hand every pipeline the same amount: the learned models ratios are memory bounds. Jin et al. (2021) report every method at matched keypoint budgets for this reason, and Barath et al. (2023) report accuracy against runtime. We therefore sweep both parameters over every pipeline on the tuning scenes first, under masking disabled and under OBB masking, and read off single matched operating point: the lowest budget at which every pipeline that can reach it is within the equivalence margin of its own saturation under both masking conditions. Masking removes the highest-contrast content in the frame, so the saturating budget need not be the same with and without it. If no budget on the grid meets the criterion, every pipeline runs at the largest one and its shortfall from saturation is reported. The thresholds are then selected at that operating point, so that what is tuned is what is run; pipeline that cannot reach it on the benchmark machine is reported as such rather than scored at lower budget. Analysis plan The plan below was fixed before the campaigns it governs ran, and the implementation applies it when it renders table, so that no number is bolded, ranked, or called difference by rule chosen after the outcome was seen. Like the comparisons of learning methods over several data sets (Demšar, 2006), it treats the independent unit, not the measurement, as the sample, and uses paired nonparametric tests over it. Units and clusters. In Part one measurement is (scene, trial) pair. The perturbation depends on the scene and the trial only, never on the pipeline, so pipelines are compared on paired per-trial differences. The independent unit is the site, of which the evaluation set has 13: two frames of one intersection from two drones show the same static scene and are not independent evidence. In Part II one measurement is frame pair under one pipeline and one masking mode. Masking is within-pair factor, since all three modes see the same pair, so the masking effect is paired difference per pair. The independent unit is the case, of which there are nine, and frame pairs within case are never treated as independent. The nine lie at seven intersections, two of them hovered over in two sessions; case is defined by the traffic at its reference frame, which two sessions do not share, so the case rather than the intersection is the unit. Outcomes. Part ranks on mAA[0, 5] of Eq. (9). The Part II masking claim has one primary contrast, OBB masking against none for the average pipeline (per case, the mean paired benefit over the pipelines measured on every outcome in every case), on five outcomes: the CTE against Hkref GCP on the audited frames, the reference-free ZNCC and gradient-orientation agreement over the evaluation region on all pairs, and intersection over union (IoU) and OCE against Hkref GCP on the audited frames. The contrast is claimed when at least one outcome favors OBB masking after Holm adjustment (Holm, 1979) across the five and none favors no masking at the unadjusted level; the second condition can only withhold claim. The outcomes differ in sensitivity: those against Hkref GCP see eight audited frames per case, the reference-free ones every pair, so requiring all five to agree would tie the claim to the least sensitive. Secondary are the same contrast per pipeline, and horizontal against none and oriented against horizontal, both for the average pipeline and per pipeline. The mechanism claim has three pre-specified contrasts, each formed within case and then read across cases: the oriented-against-none benefit increases with the coverage of the current frame; it is smaller in pairs whose foreground did not move than in pairs whose foreground did, at matched coverage (Section 7.1); and the motion alignment of Eq. (16) is larger without masking than with OBB masking. Each is read for the average pipeline, as the primary contrast is, with Holm adjustment across its outcomes (ZNCC and gradient-orientation agreement for the first two, for the third), and is supported when an outcomes interval lies above zero at an adjusted of at most 0.05; the per-pipeline readings are secondary. Capture itself is reported descriptively, per pipeline, masking mode and offset bin: the share of pairs with moving group on which the estimate is captured (Eq. (18)), the cases in which that happens, and the inlier count and ratio of captured estimates beside those of the others. It depends on the traffic each case happens to carry at its reference frame, so it describes these cases and is not tested as population rate. Estimates and intervals. Every comparison reports the paired difference as an effect size: the HodgesLehmann estimate (Hodges and Lehmann, 1963) of the per-cluster paired differences, with 95 % percentile bootstrap interval (Davison and Hinkley, 1997) obtained by resampling sites in Part and cases in Part II, with 10 000 draws. Every outcome, mAA included, is computed per cluster and differenced there, so an interval on mAA is an interval on the cluster-level paired difference. The test is an exact sign-flip permutation (Good, 2005) of the per-cluster paired differences: 213 flips in Part and 29 = 512 in Part II, so the smallest two-sided attainable in Part II is 2/512 = 0.0039. After the Holm adjustment across five outcomes, masking effect is detectable at the 0.05 level only if it has the same sign in all nine cases, or in eight with the dissenting case the smallest in magnitude (4/512 5 = 0.039). The design detects consistent effect and nothing weaker. The 2 2 over moving foreground and coherence, with two cases per cell, is reported descriptively, without intervals or an interaction test; the within-case mechanism contrasts test its prediction. Criterion for difference. difference is claimed only when the bootstrap interval excludes zero and the point estimate exceeds an equivalence margin δ, the smallest difference worth acting on (Lakens, 2017). In Part the ground truth is exact and δ = 0.01 in mAA, one percent of its [0, 1] range, so that two thousand paired trials cannot declare difference no reader would act on. In Part II, reference-relative pixel metrics use the audited residual, δ = εfloor, which for comparison pooled over the cases is the largest of the per-case residuals; pixel metrics against Hkref GCP use the 95th percentile of the GCP repeatability, the larger of the two repeat sessions; and IoU and the reference-free measures use no margin, since their units carry no floor, and are reported with intervals alone. Multiplicity and presentation. Part has one primary outcome, mAA, and Part II one primary contrast. Secondary contrasts are reported with intervals and Holm-adjusted p-values (per pipeline, across the pipelines) and mark the differences that pass the rule above, but carry no claim. Every table bolds the best value in column and every value not distinguishable from it under the rule above, and says so in its caption; columns that are diagnostics are never bolded. Bolding applies the rule without multiplicity adjustment and is descriptive: it establishes neither equivalence within the bold set nor an adjusted difference outside it. The estimate, interval and adjusted behind each of those decisions are reported in Appendix D. The correlation between inlier ratio and alignment quality  (Fig. 10)  is computed within each pipeline and case and its distribution is shown, never single pooled coefficient, because estimators differ systematically in how many inliers they report at equal accuracy (Barath et al., 2023) and pooled correlation would measure that mix. 5. Masking configurations and their annotations Three configurations are evaluated, and the complete benchmark is repeated for each: no masking, HBB masks, and OBB masks. Under the latter two, the annotated boxes of both frames are rasterized into binary mask that the feature detector receives, so that no keypoint is detected on an annotated object; an HBB is rasterized as an axis-aligned rectangle and an OBB as quadrilateral. Each box is first scaled about its center by 1 + with the mask margin = 0.15, to absorb annotation slack, shadow and motion blur at the object boundary. That margin belongs to the pipeline and is hyperparameter of it, distinct from the constant dilation τ of the evaluation region in Eq. (11), which belongs to the protocol. The HBB is the detectors and the OBB is fitted to the segmented vehicle, so the two differ in extent as well as in shape and neither need contain the other; the suppressed-area gap between the two geometries is reported for every scene set. Rationale for two box geometries. Whether the shape of mask matters for registration is not obvious in advance, and plausible mechanisms point both ways. An HBB around vehicle turned off the image axes also covers the road beside it, two wedges of asphalt that at an intersection often hold lane markings, stop lines and curb edges, the static texture the estimator most needs; the wedges grow with the angle, to about twice the vehicles own area for 4010 box at 45, and in queue of turning vehicles adjacent HBBs merge over the markings between them. OBBs keep that texture. Conversely, what moves with vehicle is not confined to its body: its cast shadow, its motion blur and the reflections off its windows travel with it, lie partly outside tight OBB, and supply correspondences that agree with its motion, and the extra area of an HBB covers part of them. Which effect dominates, if either, is an empirical question, so the box geometry is controlled axis of both parts, and the margin sweep of Section 7.5 compares the two geometries at equal suppressed area, so that difference can be told apart from the area each removes. OBBs are also what the motion axis of Section 4.4 and the object-level errors of Section 4.2 are read from, whatever the masking. 15 The annotations are the same for both parts and are produced outside the benchmark, once per image set, by the detector released with geo-trax (Fonod, 2026a) for the HBBs and by the conversion of Appendix for the oriented ones. Neither model runs inside the benchmark loop: campaign re-reads the same frames tens of thousands of times, and two pipelines are only comparable if they were handed identical masks, which per-run detector call cannot promise. Each label set carries provenance record naming the command, the settings, the package versions and the checkpoint checksums that produced it, because annotations are not bit-reproducible across accelerators and the published annotations, not the command, are the reproducible artifact. 5.1. Oriented annotations and the Songdo Vision OBB release OBB masks require an oriented annotation for every object in every frame the benchmark touches, orders of magnitude beyond what can be drawn by hand. They are obtained from the horizontal annotations by prompting SAM-family segmentation models (Kirillov et al., 2023; Ravi et al., 2025) with each box and fitting minimum-area rotated rectangle (Freeman and Shapira, 1975) to the resulting mask (Fonod, 2026b); the procedure and its validation against human-verified oriented reference are given in Appendix E. Inside the benchmark the conversion runs over the vehicle annotations of the scenes and cases under test, the only use on which any number in this paper depends. Applied to the whole of Songdo Vision (Fonod et al., 2026) at the selected configuration it yields 274 190 OBBs over 5419 frames, one per HBB and carrying its class and identifier, released as Songdo Vision OBB (Fonod and Geroliminis, 2026b) with the human-verified reference used to select and validate the conversion: 4245 OBBs over 50 frames from six recordings (Appendix E.1). None of those 50 frames appears in Songdo Vision, as checked against all 5419 by checksum and by decoded pixels, but they come from the same six flights. That is weaker guarantee than the site-level split of Section 4.7, and the appropriate one here: the conversion is selected by IoU against human-verified reference, quantity that involves neither the pipelines nor their metrics, so scene overlap cannot tune it toward favorable stabilization result; it can only flatter the reported conversion fidelity, which Appendix therefore states as tuned-set estimate. Fallback boxes. Where the segmentation finds no usable mask inside box, the source HBB is emitted unchanged, which would dilute any difference between the two mask geometries. At the selected configuration that share is 0 wherever it has been measured: among the 4245 boxes of the reference set, the 274 190 of the released conversion, and, read from the per-object confidence written beside each label file (exactly 0 marks fallback), the 2311 boxes of Part Is 29 scenes, the 60 213 of Part IIs nine cases and the 44 397 of its five tuning cases (136 frames each). 6. Part I: static benchmark 6.1. Protocol Figure 2: Part I. scene frame is warped by known geometric and photometric perturbation, and the pipeline registers the warped copy back onto the original. The perturbation is the ground truth, so no separate reference estimate is involved. The object annotations enter twice and for different purposes: as the feature mask handed to the pipeline, and as the object boxes whose object-level errors are scored. Fig. 2 shows the protocol. Known homographies (translation, rotation about the frame center, uniform scale, and small projective term) and chain of photometric degradations (brightness, saturation, blur, haze, sensor noise, and JPEG compression) are applied to static aerial frames, and the pipeline registers the degraded, warped frame back onto the original, so the ground truth is exact. Trials are paired: the perturbation of (scene, trial) does not depend on the pipeline, so every pipeline faces the identical sequence of perturbations, and every sampled parameter is recorded with its trial. The ranges (Table A.1) are those of the published campaign (Fonod et al., 2025a): translation up to 10 % of each frame dimension, rotation up to 15, scale within 5 %, and small projective term. This is wider than the deployed hover regime of Section 3, so that operating limits are measured; second configuration at deployment scale (rotation within 2, 16 translation within 2 %, scale within 1 %, no projective term, the same photometric chain) is run for the detector axis, and rotation is swept separately beyond the main range. The masks for the warped copy are the scenes boxes carried through the known homography, since the warped frame has no annotation of its own. An OBB stays quadrilateral; an HBB for the warped frame is the axis-aligned envelope of the carried OBB, which is what detector would draw around the rotated object, rather than of the carried HBB, which would inflate an envelope second time by an amount growing with the rotation. Figure 3: One trial of the detector campaign, registered again with the campaigns stored parameters and seed. (a) The evaluation scene with the most objects, every OBB outlined. (b) Its perturbed copy in trial 0, with the sampled parameters above it and random sample of unmasked ORBs inlier matches drawn between the two frames. (c, d) The dashed crop of (a) with every ORB inlier unmasked and under OBB masks, the masked area (each OBB scaled about its center by 1 + m, Table A.2) shaded; orange marks an inlier on an annotated object, blue one elsewhere. Nothing in the scene moves, so the inliers on vehicles are correct here; under masking ORB spends that share of its feature budget on the ground. Fig. 3 shows one trial. Vehicles are among the most textured content of road scene, and without masking large share of pipelines inliers lies on them. In Part that is harmless, because the vehicles move with the ground; under masking, detector that applies the mask before its keypoint cap (Section 3.2) spends that share of its budget on the ground instead. In Part II these are the correspondences moving group can contribute. The campaigns run in fixed order on the two splits of Section 4.7. On the tuning scenes: the compute-budget sweep, under masking disabled and OBB masking, which fixes the matched operating point; then the joint sweep of the ratio-test and inlier thresholds at that point. On the evaluation scenes, at the selected values: the detector axis under the three masking modes, the same axis at the untuned starting thresholds without masking, which measures the effect of tuning on data it was not selected on, the detector axis again at deployment-scale perturbation, the estimator axis at two fixed detectors, and the rotation sweep. Trial counts are 30 per scene for the tuning-side sweeps, 100 for the evaluation campaigns and 50 for the rotation sweep. Scene set and selection rule. Part runs on 29 4K frames from the hovering sessions of multi-drone experiment over the Songdo International Business District, South Korea: the static scene set of Section 3.5.2 of Fonod et al. (2025a), byte-identical to the frames that campaign ran on, whose intersections are shown in its Fig. 1. The annotation is regenerated rather than inherited, and the frames are published for the first time with the accompanying data record (Fonod and Geroliminis, 2026a). All 29 come from one session and are selected by positional rule: the first frame of the first hover of every drone-intersection pair flown in it. Each drone alternates between two or three intersections during session, and eight of the 20 intersections are covered in turn by more than one drone, so the 10 drones record them from 29 viewpoints. The set is census of the sessions viewpoints rather than sample chosen for content: no frame was kept for being busy, quiet, hard or easy, none was removed after the fact, and the rule reproduces the set from the file names alone. Table 3 describes the evaluation frames: object count and covered area each vary by factor of about four, so the masking cost is measured over range of densities, and the gap between the two area columns is how much more of the frame an HBB mask suppresses than an oriented one. Area is the fraction of the frame covered by the union of the boxes, for the oriented boxes and for the horizontal boxes they were converted from, before any mask margin; the difference between the two area columns is the additional area horizontal mask suppresses.

Results Part asks which settings of registration pipeline matter when nothing in the scene moves. The results follow the settings in the order of their effect: the compute budget, the ratio-test and inlier thresholds, and the robust estimator; then the ranking they produce at the operating point and what masking costs. The estimator, deployment and rotation sweeps are given in full in Appendix B. The compute budget sets the accuracy. The budget sweep crossed four downsampling ratios (0.18, 0.30, 0.50, 1.0) with three feature budgets (1000, 2000, 8000) on the tuning scenes, at the untuned starting thresholds, since it precedes the tuning  (Fig. 4)  , and it has the largest effect of the settings in this part. No budget met the criterion of Section 4.7, so every pipeline runs at the grids ceiling, full resolution with 8000 features, and the pipelines fall into two groups below it. ORB, XFeat, KeyNet with LightGlue, BRISK and AKAZE are still gaining at the ceiling: from half to full resolution at 8000 features their unmasked mAA rises by 0.035, 0.048, 0.023, 0.018 and 0.017, so lower operating point would rank them below their capacity. SIFT, RootSIFT, DISK and DeDoDe with LightGlue have saturated by half resolution and move by less than the equivalence margin beyond it. LoFTR, which has no feature budget, cannot reach the operating point: at full resolution it exhausts the 24 GB of the benchmark GPU (an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090) and is reported as N/A throughout Part I; below that it scores an mAA of 0.926 at ratios of 0.50 and 0.30 and 0.879 at its shipped ratio of 0.18. OBB masking changes mAA by at most 0.065 at any grid point. The largest change is ORBs gain at ratio of 0.18 with 1000 features, which shrinks to 0.017 at 2000 features and 0.004 at 8000; the largest loss is XFeats, 0.034 at full resolution with 1000 features. Since nothing in these scenes moves, any such gain is matter of which features the budget keeps, point Section 7.5 returns to. At Part IIs real-time point, six of the ten pipelines (ORB, AKAZE, XFeat, SIFT, RootSIFT and DISK with LightGlue) estimate 4K frames transform within one frame interval (33.4 ms, median over the tuning scenes) on the benchmark machine, with or without masking. The time covers downsampling, feature extraction under the mask, matching and the robust fit, not decoding, detection, box conversion or warping. The matcher thresholds have little effect at the operating point. The ratio test and the inlier threshold are the two parameters that earlier benchmarks found decisive (Efe et al., 2021; Jin et al., 2021), and they are swept jointly for every pipeline (Section 4.7), from untuned starting values: the ratio of 0.9 that the stabilization library ships and an inlier threshold of 2 to 3 px per detector, listed with the selected values in Table B.1. At the operating point the surfaces are flat. All 80 grid points of SIFT, RootSIFT, ORB, BRISK and AKAZE lie within the equivalence margin of the best, against 57 of XFeats; LightGlue applies no ratio test, so its three pipelines are swept over the threshold alone, and all 8 of their points are tied. Tuning raises mAA over the starting values by 0.0062 for XFeat and by at most 0.0011 for every other pipeline. The incumbents are the values each preset carries, and every pipeline keeps them, since no grid point beats them by more than the margin; the largest gain on offer is 0.0002, for AKAZE at ratio of 0.8. The unmasked median registration time spans factor of about thirteen: ORB and XFeat register frame in 0.10 to 0.11 s, SIFT, DISK with LightGlue and RootSIFT in 0.31 to 0.39 s, BRISK and AKAZE in 0.50 to 0.53 s, and DeDoDe and KeyNet with LightGlue in 0.84 to 1.3 s. At deployment-scale perturbation every pipeline scores higher, the leading tie set grows from four pipelines to six and no pipeline moves by more than two places. The upright learned models collapse beyond 30 of in-plane rotation (Fig. B.2), well outside the 15 of the main configuration. Both sweeps are in Appendix B. Cost of masking on static scenes. The objects in static scene move with the ground, so masking them removes correct correspondences or, for detector that refills its budget, exchanges them for others  (Fig. 3)  , and small cost is expected. This is the baseline against which the dynamic results of Section 7.5 are attributed to object motion rather than to masking as such. OBB masking costs every pipeline less than the equivalence margin. The largest loss in mAA is 0.0024, for XFeat; for the remaining eight pipelines the change is below 0.0013 in magnitude, and AKAZE, BRISK and KeyNet with LightGlue gain up to 0.0012. HBB masking costs as little: 0.0024 for XFeat and at most 0.0008 for the other eight pipelines, two of which gain. It scores below OBB masking for every pipeline but AKAZE, as the larger mask predicts (a median of 3.56 % of the frame against 3.32 %, Table 3), but by at most 0.0007, so at these object densities the extra area 20 an HBB removes costs almost nothing, and difference between the two mask shapes in the dynamic benchmark is not explained by the area they remove alone. 7. Part II: dynamic benchmark 7.1. Protocol Figure 5: Part II. Every candidate registers the same frame pairs under each masking mode in turn, and the reference estimator registers them once, under OBB masks. The reference estimator supplies pseudo-ground truth and its own error is measured against GCPs; that residual is the equivalence margin of the reference-relative pixel metrics. On the audited frames homography fitted to the same points is an independent reference of its own, and the identity transform is scored on every pair as the unstabilized baseline. The object annotations enter as the feature mask and, placed by the reference estimator, as the evaluation region and as the object motion that the capture fraction is read against. Fig. 5 shows the protocol and Table A.3 its constants. case is one hover, the recording of one drone over one intersection cut to its stable part, which lasts two to four minutes (Fonod et al., 2025a), and every sampled frame of it is registered directly onto one reference frame, as the deployed pipeline does. The reference is frame the case selection picks inside the hover rather than its first: traffic at an intersection comes in phases, and whether group of vehicles moving together is in view at the reference decides whether capture can occur at all. Temporal offsets run up to 3600 frames (2 min at 29.97 frames per second) in twelve bins one octave wide, 1, 23, 47, 815, and so on to 10242047 and 20483600 frames, with 15 pairs drawn in each bin that holds that many and every offset of the four shortest, 135 pairs per case, each weighing the same. The spacing follows the mechanism. Capture needs objects present in both frames that moved together, and both conditions decay fast: in the Songdo Traffic trajectories (Fonod et al., 2025b), over all 20 intersections and 4 days, about 90 % of the vehicles in view at given instant are still in view 4 later, 64 % after 16 s, 45 % after 32 s, 22 % after 64 and 5 % after 120 (lower bounds, since the ends of hover cut some stays short), and the members of moving group drift apart within seconds. Evenly spaced offsets would spend most pairs on frames that share no moving group with the reference and average the effect away; the octaves resolve the shortest offsets, where group is still shared and still moves as one, and the results are read per bin. Every pipeline of Part is candidate, so that ranking that changes between static and dynamic footage can be observed rather than assumed away, and every candidate runs under all three masking modes on every pair, so masking is within-pair factor. SIFT, the reference estimators own detector, is among them, which makes the one pairing that is circular by construction (Section 4.8) explicit. The candidates run in two regimes, both points of Part Is budget grid  (Fig. 4)  . The offline regime, for registering recorded video after the flight, is half resolution with 2000 features, the operating point of the campaign this work extends (Fonod et al., 2025a). The real-time regime is the grids cheapest point, downsampling ratio of 0.18 with 1000 features, at which six of the ten pipelines estimate frames transform within one frame interval (33.4 ms) at the median on the benchmark machine. In both, the inlier threshold is given in pixels of the downsampled frame, so that it keeps its size relative to keypoint localization. The regimes share the cases, the pairs, the reference estimator and the GCPs; the mask-margin sweep and the repeated runs are made in the offline regime only. Two further rows are scored on every pair without any pipeline: the identity, which is the unstabilized frame and the transform failed pipeline delivers, and the reference estimator itself. 21 Thresholds are tuned again in each regime. The ratio-test and inlier thresholds are not carried over from Part I, where they were selected under synthetic warps of static scenes: moving objects change which correspondences are outliers, and the inlier threshold in particular decides whether matches on moving group join the consensus. They are tuned in each regime by Part Is procedure and selection rule, with Part Is values as the incumbents (a joint grid widened to 14 ratios from 0.4 to 0.99 and 13 inlier thresholds from 0.1 to 16 px, selected on mAA, masking disabled), scored against the reference estimator on five tuning cases that the survey selects, one per cell and one control, from the intersections of Part Is tuning scenes, so that no tuning case shares an intersection with an evaluation case. Offline, SIFT, BRISK and AKAZE move to the strictest corner of the grid, = 0.40 and θ = 0.1 px, and XFeat to = 0.45 and θ = 8 px, gaining 0.0102 to 0.0156 mAA on the tuning cases; in real time ORB, AKAZE, XFeat, DISK+LightGlue and DeDoDe+LightGlue move, gaining 0.0100 to 0.1249; the others keep Part Is values (Tables C.1 and C.2). The selections at an end of the grid are not followed past it: the offline ones agree with the reference estimator to median of 0.08 px to 0.20 px, and the margin of 0.01 mAA corresponds to about 0.05 px of error, both well below the audited floor (Section 4.8), so stricter setting could only gain agreement with the reference that the audit cannot resolve. The same holds for AKAZEs θ = 0.1 px in real time (0.45 px); ORBs real-time = 0.99 lies next to = 1, where the ratio test no longer rejects anything. The thresholds selected without masking are then used under all three masking modes, so measured masking advantage is not inflated by the tuning. Cases are selected from the video alone. The hypothesis predicts when capture is severe: where more of the foreground moves, and moves coherently. Testing that needs footage spanning those conditions, so the nine cases are selected by design, on the amount and the coherence of the moving foreground as measured from the video. The candidates come from the hovers of one recording day at the evaluation sites of Part Is split; the next day in fixed order is added only if cell cannot be filled. Every hover is read at points 30 apart, clear of its first and last seconds and with the full 3600 frames after them, and each point is candidate reference frame; hover supplies at most one case. Joint reading of the two protocols Part ranks pipelines against exact truth on static scenes and shows which of their settings matter there: the compute budget, by wide margin, then the estimators threshold for estimators that commit to one, while the matcher thresholds have little effect at the operating point and masking costs almost nothing. Part II asks whether that ranking survives footage in which part of the frame moves. Capture predicts specific pattern: pipeline falls without masking, recovers under masking, and has its error along the motion while unmasked, with capture fraction near one on the pairs that carry moving group. The data show that pattern for ORB at the real-time budget: its unmasked estimates follow the group with 35 capture fraction up to 0.96 within the surveys offsets  (Fig. 1)  , and its error along the motion rises; the alignment rises little, since the captures are few percent of the pairs. Its fall from 0.6785 masked to 0.5835 unmasked is mostly not on the captured pairs, which bound their share of it at 0.023, and the rest is of the size of the budget effect, which masking has on static scenes as well (Section 7.5). For the other pipelines the static ranking carries over: SIFT, RootSIFT and AKAZE lead Part II in both regimes, masked or not. The static masking cost is the control that makes that reading possible: in Part the annotated objects satisfy the same homography as the background, so suppressing them cannot improve the consensus, only change which correspondences the budget keeps. 8.3. Practical guidance No single pipeline is called best. The leading tie set on mAA is AKAZE, RootSIFT, SIFT and BRISK under the main Part configuration and grows to six pipelines at deployment-scale perturbation; beyond 30 of rotation the upright learned models drop out (Fig. B.2). In Part II the tie set against the reference is SIFT, RootSIFT and AKAZE under every masking mode in both regimes; against the GCPs every configuration ties at the median in both, and at the 90th percentile all but ORB in real time  (Fig. 11)  . Offline, masking offers little practitioner could act on: every configuration lies within the repeatability of the GCPs, and the masking benefits are tenths of pixel or less. In real time it makes ORB usable, at cost on static scenes of less than 0.005 mAA. For real-time pipeline the choice is open: masked ORB registers in 12 to 13 ms at median error of 1.17 to 1.19 px against the GCPs, and SIFT, RootSIFT and AKAZE, masked or not, in 18 to 22 ms at 0.51 to 0.57 px; all fit one frame interval at the median, and for the latter three masking changes background alignment by less than 0.001 in either direction, which no contrast resolves (Tables 9, 11 and 13). Compute excludes some pipelines on its own: LoFTR cannot run at Part Is full resolution on the benchmark GPU, and four of the ten (BRISK, LoFTR, and DeDoDe and KeyNet with LightGlue) need more than one frame interval at the real-time point. HBBs and OBBs do not differ measurably for registration at these densities and orientations, in the masking contrasts or in the margin sweep; road grid oblique to the image, larger vehicles at lower altitude or long turning queues would give the geometry more room to matter, and the protocol measures it there unchanged. OBBs remain useful elsewhere, in the motion axis of Section 4.4 and in object-level errors that respect an objects extent. SIFT and the learned detectors apply the mask after selecting their keypoints in the library evaluated here (Section 3.2), so for them masking can only remove keypoints; selecting after the mask is change to the library, which the protocol would measure unchanged. 8.4. Limitations Coverage of the cases. The cases come from one recording day at one altitude band, and their moving foreground at the reference covers at most 1.94% of the frame, so what is found about capture holds for that range. Each case is registered onto one reference frame, chosen to span the conditions capture depends on; how often capture occurs over all the frames deployed pipeline might register onto is different quantity, which the design does not estimate. Part II has nine independent units at seven intersections: masking effect is detectable only if it has the same sign in all of them, or in eight with the dissenting case the smallest, and the 2 2 with two cases per cell is descriptive. Taking the intersection as the unit leaves every claim unchanged, but the per-pipeline benefits that meet the rule fall short of it, since seven units cannot pass Holms adjustment over ten pipelines, and ORBs real-time coverage correlation loses its interval above zero. Cases with larger moving share, from lower altitudes or congested approaches, and more sites and sessions are the most informative extension; the selection procedure is automated so that they can be added without revisiting the design. Resolution of the ground control points. The GCPs are repeatable to 1.00 px at the 95th percentile. They separate captured estimate from correct one and give masking contrast independent of the reference, but they cannot rank pipelines whose errors differ by less than pixel, and the reference-relative columns, which can, are limited by the audited residual. With eight audited frames per case, the GCPs see only the few captured estimates that fall on one (Section 7.3); the capture fraction, read against the reference on every pair, is what counts them. The reference estimator is member of the family under test, run with OBB masking; its absolute error is measured by the audit, but not its covariance with candidates, which is why the masking comparison is read from the GCPs and the reference-free measures. Budget, resolution and scene. Part IIs two regimes change the resolution and the feature budget together; Part separates the two on static scenes  (Fig. 4)  , and the mask-margin sweep was run in the offline regime only. Part Is 29 scenes come from one session on one day, so the split prevents tuning on the evaluation scenes but does not make the session representative of other cities, altitudes or lighting. The registration model is single homography: buildings, raised structures and large tree canopy are excluded from the reference-free measures, but poles, signs and isolated street trees are not, and their parallax grows with the platforms drift, which within hover is small and is the same for every candidate. Footage from translating platform, or with tall structure filling much of the frame, needs different registration model. Annotations and object classes. The OBBs come from segmentation-based conversion (Appendix E); its fallback share is zero on this benchmarks image sets, and where it is not, comparison between the two box geometries is diluted by it. Most of the benchmark is indifferent to what the objects are, but two parts assume vehicles: the motion axis is recovered from the long axes of OBBs, which holds for vehicles and vessels and not for people, and the coherence descriptor assumes population that moves as streams. Both degrade to an undefined axis and an unfilled cell rather than to wrong number. 9. Conclusion Coherently moving objects can capture the geometric consensus of robust estimator, and the statistics that describe fits self-consistency would then describe the wrong fit. This paper turns that possibility into measurement for the complete registration pipeline used in reference-frame stabilization of hovering-drone video. static protocol under exact ground truth establishes what each pipeline can do. dynamic protocol on nine intersection cases, each registered onto reference frame selected from the video alone, measures what the same pipelines do when part of the frame moves, at an offline and real-time budget, with ground-control-point audit that measures the error of the pseudo-ground-truth reference and scores every candidate independently of it. On static scenes, four tuned classical pipelines (AKAZE, RootSIFT, SIFT, BRISK) lead; the compute budget decides accuracy far more than the matcher thresholds, which MAGSAC++ makes nearly irrelevant, and masking costs every pipeline less than 0.005 mAA. On the dynamic cases unmasked ORB is captured in real time in every case that presents coherently moving group, on 28 of 304 real-time pairs and 6 offline, and the estimates pulled toward group have the inlier statistics of the same pipeline at the nearest offsets. Object masking removes capture for every pipeline at both budgets and restores ORB in real time, though the captured pairs can account for at most quarter of that gain; it leaves the leading pipelines (SIFT, RootSIFT, AKAZE) unchanged, and HBBs and OBBs do not differ at these densities and orientations, where the two withhold nearly the same pixels. How capture scales with the moving share, from lower altitudes or over congested approaches, is the question the benchmark is built to answer next. The protocol needs only annotated boxes for the objects and dozen or so GCPs on each of handful of frames per case. The benchmark implementation, the data every reported number is computed from, the OBB dataset and the human-verified reference that validates its conversion are released so that the comparison can be extended to other pipelines, other platforms and other classes of moving object without changing the protocol. Appendix E. Horizontal-to-oriented box conversion The OBBs are converted from the HBBs by hbb2obb (Fonod, 2026b). This appendix summarizes the procedure, selection and accuracy, which Songdo Vision OBB (Fonod and Geroliminis, 2026b) documents in full with the commands that reproduce them. Procedure. Each HBB, its sides moved outward by scale factor of its width and height (each dimension grows by 2s), prompts one or more SAM-family models (Kirillov et al., 2023; Ravi et al., 2025), and an ensembles masks are combined by majority vote. The mask is cropped to the scaled prompt and refined by signed morphological step (Soille, 2004), its square kernel set fraction of the shorter side of the largest contours bounding rectangle: positive kernel opens it, removing thin protrusion such as an overhead sign enclosed by the box, and negative kernel closes it, rejoining body split by glare or an occluder. minimum-area rotated rectangle (Freeman and Shapira, 1975) is fitted to the largest contour together with any piece holding at least set fraction of its area. The OBB keeps the class of its HBB; where no valid mask is found, the HBB is emitted unchanged, the fallback whose consequence is stated in Section 5. Selection. The ensemble, the inference resolution, the prompt scale factor and the signed kernel fraction interact, so they were selected by grid search against the human-verified reference of Appendix E.1: eleven model configurations, each at 45 grid points (resolution {896, 1024, 1152}, scale factor {0.01, 0, 0.01, 0.02, 0.03}, kernel {0.10, 0, +0.10}), 495 conversions of the 50 reference frames. Mean IoU saturates on tightly fitted boxes: the three leading configurations lie within 0.44 standard errors of one another (Table E.1 and Fig. E.1). Configurations within one standard error of the leader are treated as tied, heuristic rather than test, and ties are broken by the share of boxes below IoU 0.75 and the 90th-percentile orientation error, taking the cheapest configuration that leads on both. That is single sam_l at resolution 1024, with scale factor of 0.02 and closing whose kernel is 0.1 of that side, at 39 % of the inference cost of the leading ensemble. 49 Accuracy. On the reference, the selected configuration reaches mean IoU of 0.886 79 (standard error 0.001 43), median of 0.917 59, 92.1 % of boxes above IoU 0.75 and 61.5 % above 0.90, and 90th-percentile orientation error of 3.50, measured on the frames it was selected on, with exact prompts (Appendix E.1). With perturbed copies it loses at most 0.002 of mean IoU while the expanded prompt still covers the vehicle, 0.027 under 2 px center jitter and 0.043 once the prompt falls short. On the 1345 vehicles turned off the image axes it raises mean IoU over the HBB itself from 0.6032 to 0.8039 and improves on it for 91.9 % of them; over the whole set the 90th-percentile orientation error falls from 22.69 to 3.50.
